children: Major US law firms are continuing to scoop up lawyers from Weil, Gotshal & Manges, including more than a dozen new partner hires by Skadden, Simpson Thacher, Dechert and Kirkland & Ellis, amid the New York-based firm's dissolution.

Weil ​lawyers are scattering following the firm’s decision this month to wind down operations, boosting partnerships at its onetime competitors. Partners at Weil voted last week to dissolve the firm after mounting departures, cementing the fall of a 95-year-old law firm that helped steer high-profile bankruptcies, corporate takeovers and litigation for decades.

The moves ​add to an already busy hiring market for law firms that's been supercharged by Weil's collapse. Earlier this week Cleary Gottlieb, Paul Hastings and Skadden said they were bringing on other lawyers from Weil.

Skadden said on Wednesday it was adding a team of seven intellectual property litigators from Weil, including Douglas Lumish and Jeff Homrig, who co-led the firm's IP, technology & science litigation group. Lumish and Homrig will co-lead Skadden's IP litigation group, the firm said.

Lumish and Homrig defended Meta Platforms in a lawsuit claiming the Facebook parent infringed on a Dutch software company's patents related to a system for auto-completing search prompts. Meta reached a confidential settlement in the case in 2024.
Simpson Thacher said it was adding five Weil partners to its ranks, including John Barry, who led its employment practice. Barry will now lead Simpson Thacher's employment practice, the firm said.

Dechert said it hired corporate partner Nandan Nelivigi and tax partner Michael Sykes from Weil. Nelivigi works on deals involving major energy and infrastructure projects, while Sykes advises on tax incentives and financing strategies for energy projects, Dechert said.
Kirkland said Weil tax partner Lauren Gorsche will be joining the firm.

Weil's decision to wind down has forced a scramble among both its lawyers and non-attorney staffers. In California, the firm said it will be eliminating more than 100 jobs, according to a series of Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification Act (WARN) notices filed with the state.
